newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway peacekeepers up in arms over extra tax.
newsitem.headline: Norway peacekeepers up in arms over extra tax.

text.p: Hundreds of Norwegian peacekeepers in Bosnia and Lebanon handed in their resignations at the weekend in an unprecedented protest against an extra income tax that was suddenly slapped on them, officials said on Sunday.
Defence Minister Joergen Kosmo, reacting promptly to the mass resignations, pledged to strike a deal with the finance ministry within a week so that no soldier would lose any money.
"I am confident we can solve this," he told Norwegian radio.
The peacekeepers, both privates and officers, stuck to their guns and demanded proof before withdrawing the resignations.
"Everyone from the private soldier to the general is in on this action," Tore Kvalheim, spokesman for Norway's association of military officers (BFO), told Reuters.

He said a sergeant earned an average 300,000 crowns ($42,200) a year and was taxed between 30 to 40 percent on the income. Soldiers stand to lose between 30,000 and 55,000 crowns a year each because of the new rule, he said.
"We feel betrayed. This was not the agreement we made. We have never before protested as strongly as now. We feel the people at the finance ministry don't know what they are doing.
"They look at numbers but don't see the obligations Norway has in the international community," Kvalheim said.

The soldiers, the pride of Norway's acclaimed commitment to international peacekeeping, learned on Friday that the finance ministry had decided to tax, retroactively from January 1, an allowance paid to soldiers working overseas.

The fringe benefit, granted to overseas soldiers to compensate for extra expenses resulting from living abroad, was previously exempt from taxation, but the ministry said this was wrong and had to be corrected.
About 1,600 Norwegians are serving in peacekeeping missions for NATO and the United Nations in Bosnia and Lebanon.
Around 650 Norwegians in Bosnia and more than 300 in Lebanon tendered their resignations on Saturday in response to getting the overseas allowance taxed, Kvalheim said.
"Kosmo's declaration is all well but the resignations will not be withdrawn until we see what he is putting on the table. Everyone is ready to go home if the tax is applied."

Kosmo said he would either have the finance ministry retain the tax exemption on overseas allowances or, failing that, order compensation for the soldiers for the loss of income incurred by the new ruling. ($ = 7.108 Norwegian Crowns)
